title: Why Robert Maillart Made Concrete Arches Hollow
topic: Why the Swiss engineer Robert Maillart designed concrete arches with hollow boxes (Switzerland, 1910)

lines: Robert Maillart walked across his own bridges to test them.
He rarely tested a bridge before construction.
He checked the finished bridge by crossing it himself.
Before 1900, engineers used shapes that were easy to analyze with mathematics.
Maillart preferred common sense to predict how a full-size bridge would behave.
His designs went beyond the common boundaries of concrete design.
So Maillart combined the road deck with the arch ribs.
That created one closely integrated structure of very thin concrete.
You see, Maillart's hollow arch was like a cardboard box: light in your hands, yet hard to twist.
A box has multiple walls, so it resists twisting better than an I-beam.
At the same height, a box carries more load than an I-beam.
Concrete carried compression, which means squeezing.
Steel bars carried tension, which means pulling.
His Salginatobel proposal won a competition partly for its low cost.
In 2001, a British trade journal voted Salginatobel 'the most beautiful bridge of the century.'
And Maillart checked his work the hard way: by crossing the bridge himself.

claims.claim: Maillart rarely tested his bridges before construction and often tested them by crossing them himself.
Before the 1900s engineers used shapes that could be analyzed easily using mathematics, while Maillart preferred common sense and visualization to predict full-scale performance.
Maillart's designs went beyond the common boundaries of concrete design in his time.
Maillart combined the deck and arch ribs into closely integrated structures of very thin reinforced concrete and concrete slabs.
Maillart's hollow-box technique was used to overcome large spans.
A box girder forms an enclosed tube with multiple walls, better resists torsion than an I-beam, and can carry more load than an I-beam of equal height.
Concrete carried compressive forces while steel bars carried tension forces.
Maillart's Salginatobel proposal was selected from nineteen entrants in a design competition partly because of its low cost.
In 2001 the British trade journal Bridge - Design and Engineering voted Salginatobel 'the most beautiful bridge of the century'.
